_convention: Keep every string here DEFINITIONAL: what a number measures and how to read
it. No observations about a particular week ('three spikes carry the month'),
no named users, no incident write-ups. Those age badly and a rerun cannot
refresh them; put that kind of analysis in a blog post or issue instead.
Anything that is really a derived statistic should be a {{token}} rather than
a typed-in number (see STAT_TOKENS in scripts/insights.mjs).
title: cdg2mp4 — usage
headline: Conversion analytics
lede: Everything the converter records, covering {{rangeFromLong}} to {{rangeToLong}}. The tool runs entirely in the browser, so these are anonymous counts of events, not accounts. Each panel says what it measures and how to read it.
cumNote: Every completed conversion since tracking began. Read the slope, not the height: a near-vertical stretch is usually one person working through a disc collection rather than a jump in how many people are using the tool. Check it against the profiles chart before treating it as growth.
dailyNote: Completed conversions per day. Because a single person can run dozens in a session, a tall bar is a usage-depth signal, not an audience signal. The busiest day here is {{topDay}}.
idsNote: Browser profiles seen, accumulating. This is the closest thing to an audience curve: it moves when new people arrive, and stays flat while an existing user is mid-batch. The dashed line drops my own testing and traffic from cloud datacenter ranges.
caveatEyebrow: Read this before quoting a user count
caveatHeading: A profile is not a person
caveatNote: PostHog identifies anonymous visitors with a per-browser ID kept in local storage, and this app never calls identify, so nothing is ever merged across devices. One ID means one browser profile that still has its storage. The same person counts twice across two browsers, across a laptop and a phone, or after clearing site data. Treat the total as an upper bound, and the “completed at least one conversion” row as the only one that reflects real use.
breakdownNote: What the {{profiles}} profiles are actually made of. Only the first row used the tool for its purpose.
breakdownAfter: Even the converted row overstates the number of humans: profiles created minutes apart in the same city, on the same operating system, are usually one person on two machines. A realistic headcount is somewhat below {{converted}}.
failNote: Failed attempts per day, {{failed}} of {{started}} in total. A cluster from very few profiles usually means one machine cannot run the converter at all, which repeats on every visit; a spread across many profiles is more likely a real regression. The table names the causes.
failTableNote: Grouped by the reason code the app assigns and the stage it failed at. bad_input and the zip_missing_* codes are user-side (the wrong files were dropped). load_failed means the converter never started, which points at the browser or the network rather than the file.
footer: Events are anonymous: no accounts, no file contents, no identities. Filenames and coarse IP geolocation are recorded; the conversion itself runs entirely in the browser and files are never uploaded. “Self” is my own testing; “datacenter” is bot and scanner traffic from cloud regions. Generated {{generatedOn}} by npm run insights from data through {{rangeToLong}}.
